title: Hosted conversation API: streaming basics, params & retry walkthrough
summary:
Discovery/demo hybrid: quick hosted API chat/text generation walkthrough covering streaming behavior, common tunables (temperature, max_tokens, stop tokens), backoff/retry strategies, idempotency and basic console hints. Customer cares about latency for live chat, cost per 1k tokens, and SOC2 + VPC options. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot and share security docs and pricing.
Notes: transcript has occasional mis-heards (K-V cash, S0C2).
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-21 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 mins
Attendees: Avery Chen, Samir Patel (Redwood); Lena Ortiz, Marcus Lin, Priya Shah, Evan Brooks (Marigold)

[00:00] Avery: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for making the time. Avery from Redwood, i'll kick us off and then Samir will do a live run through of the hosted chat API and console.
[00:16] Lena: thanks, quick context — we're building an in-app triage chat for patients, needs to feel realtime, under 300ms ideally on average per token, and must be audited for compliance.
[00:29] Marcus: and just to add, our infra is on aws; we currently use managed endpoints but want better cost predictability.
[00:40] Avery: perfect; i'll show the hosted path first — low effort, quick to iterate. Samir, take it away.
[00:45] Samir: cool, starting with the api call pattern. single request/streaming response. we'll demo streaming where client gets tokens as produced. code sample: fetch to /v1/chat/completions (note: transcript auto replaces exact path sometimes). streaming is server-sent events, you get delta chunks.
[01:15] Samir: important tunables — temperature, top_p, max_tokens, presence/penalty; set temperature to 0.2 for deterministic clinical style, increase for creative copy. max_tokens limits completion length, stop tokens help cut off trailing polite closers.
[01:42] Marcus: what about billing when streaming? do we pay for partial responses if we stop early?
[01:50] Avery: we bill on tokens emitted + input tokens; if you cut the stream early you pay for tokens sent. There's also embedding/unit costs for other endpoints.
[02:10] Evan: security question: does hosted keep transcripts? we need data retention and SAML and SOC compliance.
[02:21] Samir: yes so hosted has retention controls and enterprise tiers include audit logs, SSO (saml) integration, and SOC2 docs — we'll send the security pack. for highly regulated flows you can use Dedicated or Private VPC.
[02:45] Priya: can you run through retries — we're worried about transient errors during a long stream.
[02:52] Samir: sure. streaming retries are usually done client-side: if a stream breaks mid-response, best practice is to retry with an idempotency token and request from the last confirmed token offset. we recommend tracking the last confirmed delta and re-sending a prompt prefix. Redwood's SDKs surface helpers for reconnect and delta-replay.
[03:30] Lena: sounds complex, can you show a simple example?
[03:35] Samir: yes. example flow: 1) start stream with idempotency key X 2) if disconnect at token N, resume by appending cached context to new request and pass same key so the platform can detect duplicates; we also expose a partial-response checksum to validate continuity. note: some of the names in SDK are slightly different in the UI, e.g., KV cache sometimes shows as K-V cash in logs — small transcript quirk.
[04:10] Marcus: what's the recommended backoff policy?
[04:14] Samir: exponential with jitter, typical base 500ms, cap at 8s, and limit attempts to 4 for user-facing flows so UX isn't degraded. for background jobs you can be more aggressive. we demo a small retry helper in the client repo.
[04:45] Samir: switching to params demo — lowering max_tokens and using stop sequences reduces cost and keeps responses on-point. also use result-stream sampling: set temperature low and deterministic tokens.
[05:12] Priya: how do we measure latency in the console?
[05:16] Avery: the console shows per-route mean p50/p95 latency, token breakdown, and per-token cost. you can filter by token type. we'll show the trace view in a sec.
[05:35] Samir: quick note on batch and cache: Redwood Optimize suggests batching similar short requests and prefix caching for repeated system prompts to cut token spend. for conversational UIs caching earlier system messages is common.
[06:00] Lena: do you have numbers for how batching affects latency? that's a big worry.
[06:06] Samir: batching trades off latency for throughput; for real-time chat you want small batch sizes or continuous batching with tight latency SLOs. e.g., batching 8x reduces per-token cost but can add 50–200ms depending on queuing window and model.
[06:30] Marcus: and quantization — can that reduce cost while keeping accuracy?
[06:35] Samir: yes, model quantization recommendations from Optimize: int8 quant works for many gen flows, sometimes with minor quality drop; our recommend engine automatically picks kernel paths. we'll send a small eval showing you quality delta on your dataset.
[06:58] Priya: show us the console please.
[07:03] Samir: (screen) Console > Routes > chat-gen-demo. here you can see per-route metrics, token cost breakdown, streaming trace: each request shows handshake, first token latency, and total completion time. you can also configure retention for logs.
[07:42] Samir: open the trace for a sample user: you can see streaming frames; time between first byte and subsequent tokens; in a failing stream you'll see a disconnect event and reason code.
[08:05] Marcus: how to instrument retries in our client?
[08:09] Samir: we have SDK helpers for auto-reconnect, idempotency token generation, and delta-replay; there's also guidance in the docs for idempotency semantics — short, stateless replays are safest.
[08:30] Lena: any gotchas for web mobile clients?
[08:34] Samir: mobile can have flakier networks — we recommend small window batching and SDK reconnect. plus use horns for tokenization so you don't double-charge tokens by re-sending long context. (note: 'horns' is a mis-transcription — meant 'hunks' or 'chunks').
[09:02] Evan: security again — where are keys stored for hosted vs private?
[09:07] Avery: hosted: keys in our key vault, rotated by default; enterprise customers can use KMS integrations. Private deployments let you manage keys in HSM/KMS behind your VPC. we'll include our KMS integration guide.
[09:28] Priya: show an example request with streaming and reconnection.
[09:33] Samir: code snippet: POST /v1/chat.stream with header Accept: text/event-stream; body includes messages array, temperature, max_tokens, idempotency-key. on reconnect send prefix, set resume:true, pass last_token_index. the platform will detect duplicate tokens if same idempotency key used.
[10:05] Marcus: what about long running conversations — do we send entire history each time?
[10:10] Samir: best practice: keep a sliding window of recent turns in the prompt; store embeddings of older turns and fetch summaries or compressed context on the fly. Optimize recommends using prefix cache for static system instructions.
[10:35] Lena: how does Redwood's runtime handle KV cache for the model?
[10:39] Samir: the runtime manages KV cache per session for fast next-token generation. sometimes in logs it's listed as K-V cash, minor name mismatch. KV cache avoids recomputing transformer states for prefix tokens, which lowers latency.
[11:02] Priya: show failover — what happens when a model variant is down?
[11:07] Samir: smart routing: requests can fall back to a compatible cheaper variant if the preferred model is unavailable; you can configure fallback chains and match quality thresholds. there are also region fallback policies to keep low latency.
[11:30] Marcus: curious on how you do continuous batching without hurting latency.
[11:34] Samir: the runtime uses adaptive batching windows: it waits a few ms for more inflight requests but releases if latency budget is hit; kernel selection also helps since some kernels are much faster at small seq lengths.
[12:05] Avery: switching to a quick demo on retries in practice — Samir will intentionally kill the stream to show reconnect.
[12:12] Samir: (demo) starting stream... streaming tokens... kill connection... re-establish... client resumes with idempotency key X and prefix of last 200 tokens, platform dedups. you can see in the console trace an event "resume_success" and a small delta replay.
[13:00] Priya: great. what's the usual token cost range we'd see for a 3-turn exchange with 50 token responses?
[13:06] Avery: rough ballpark: input tokens ~120, output ~150 => ~270 tokens per interaction; at hosted pricing that's X cents per 1k, we'll give exact bucketed pricing in the follow up.
[13:30] Marcus: are there quotas and rate limits?
[13:33] Avery: yes, per-tenant quotas exist and can be raised for enterprise. burst policies and reserved capacity are available via Dedicated.
[13:50] Evan: audit log granularity — can we see token-level traces in logs?
[13:55] Samir: audit logs show request metadata, trace ids and optionally deltas; full transcripts are stored only if retention is enabled. for strict compliance you can ship logs to your SIEM.
[14:20] Lena: timeline — we want to pilot in the next 2 weeks, 2-week POC to validate latency and cost.
[14:28] Avery: sounds good. next steps we'll outline.
[14:32] Samir: quick Optimize note — we can auto-suggest batching/cache profiles from your early traffic in a test window; usually within 48 hours you see suggestions.
[14:50] Priya: any competitors you see for specific private deployments?
[14:55] Avery: they mentioned names in earlier calls; common competitors: Major Cloud Managed Endpoints, InferCo (misspoken), and other LLM APIs. we'll include competitive note.
[15:12] Marcus: ok let's map owners.
[15:15] Avery: wrap up and action items next.
[15:18] (rest of call — planning and Q&A, 26 more minutes, snippets)
[16:00] Priya: can you share a sample benchmark sheet so we can map per-call cost?
[16:05] Avery: yes, sending pricing + benchmark template.
[17:22] Samir: also sending a small script to reproduce the reconnect demo.
[20:05] Evan: security team will review SOC2 and SAML docs, expect questions on key rotation cadence.
[23:40] Marcus: we'll provision a sandbox account and send a sample dataset for eval.
[26:11] Avery: we'll schedule a kickoff for the pilot next monday; Samir to lead tech onboarding.
[33:00] Lena: thanks everyone, that was helpful.
[33:12] Avery: thanks all — we'll follow up with docs and links.

End transcript (note: timestamps are approximate and some terms mis-transcribed).
